Slovak Agriculture Hit by Canadian Tariffs as Exporters Face Mounting Losses

BRATISLAVA, June 27 – Canadian tariffs imposed this month on grain and meat imports from Slovakia are disrupting the country’s agriculture industry, with producers warning of layoffs and financial strain as exports stall at the border.

Canada introduced the new tariffs, ranging from 15% to 25%, on Slovak wheat, barley, pork and beef, citing what Ottawa called an “unfair competitive advantage” stemming from recent Slovak agricultural subsidies. The measures went into effect June 10 and are expected to continue for at least 60 days pending further review.

Slovakia’s agriculture ministry estimates that more than 18,000 tonnes of grain and 2,500 tonnes of pork and beef, previously destined for Canadian buyers, are now being stored in silos and warehouses across the country. “Producers are facing immediate cash-flow problems,” said Martina Kováčová, spokesperson for the Slovak Agriculture Chamber. “Many farms depend on stable access to the Canadian market, which has now been effectively closed to them.”

Officials at the ministry say that nearly 3,000 jobs in rural areas could be at risk if the tariffs remain in place through the summer. “We are already seeing reduced shifts at several meat-processing sites in the east, and some smaller grain cooperatives are considering temporary closures,” said Peter Mihálik, head of operations at Danubia Farms, a major Slovak exporter.

Analysts note that the Canadian market accounts for about 12% of Slovakia’s agricultural exports outside the European Union. “The sudden loss of this outlet is putting severe downward pressure on local prices for both grain and meat,” said Zuzana Urbanová, an agriculture economist at Bratislava University. “Producers are being forced to sell domestically at a loss or store unsold goods, increasing costs and uncertainty.”

Slovak officials are seeking talks with Canadian counterparts to resolve the dispute, while industry groups urge government support for affected farms and workers. “We need urgent action to prevent permanent damage to our agriculture sector,” said Kováčová. The tariffs remain in effect as negotiations continue.
